intro: Humboldt Redwoods State Park in northern California holds Rockefeller Forest, the largest remaining continuous old-growth coast redwood forest in the world. Two of its named giants stand in the Big Tree Area on Bull Creek: the Giant Tree, national champion coast redwood in 1991 at 363 feet, and the Tall Tree, 359 feet when measured in 1957. Both are free to walk to on short trails.

trees.name: The Giant Tree

location.address: Big Trees Loop, Big Tree Area, Bull Creek, Rockefeller Forest, Humboldt Redwoods State Park, California

trees.story:
In November 1991 the American Forestry Association named this coast redwood the national champion of its species, and the park's sign beside it still gives the figures. It is 363 feet tall, about 110 metres, with a trunk 53.2 feet round, about 16 metres, and an average crown spread of 62 feet. Save the Redwoods League explains that the title goes to the best combination of height, trunk and crown, not to height alone.

It stands in Rockefeller Forest, the part of Humboldt Redwoods State Park that holds the largest remaining continuous old-growth coast redwood forest in the world. Settlers began felling the redwoods here in the 1850s and the timber industry followed. The park began in 1921, when Save the Redwoods League bought land largely from the Pacific Lumber Company, and only about five percent of the old coast redwood forest survives anywhere.

Nobody has published an age for it. The reader who sent it to us filed it as a giant sequoia, but the park's own sign names it Sequoia sempervirens, the coast redwood. It is on the Big Trees Loop by the Big Tree Area parking on Bull Creek, in the same grove as the Tall Tree, and it costs nothing to stand at its foot and look up.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the black park sign in front of it naming it the Giant Tree, national champion coast redwood. It stands on the Big Trees Loop by the Big Tree Area parking on Bull Creek.

trees.name: The Tall Tree

location.address: Bull Creek Flat, Rockefeller Forest, Humboldt Redwoods State Park, California

trees.story:
When this coast redwood was measured in February 1957 it stood 359.3 feet tall, about 109.5 metres, and the sign the park put beside it still says so. The same sign gives a trunk 42 feet round at breast height, almost 13 metres, and 13.4 feet across. Redwood writers call it the Rockefeller Tall Tree and say it once held the title of the world's tallest known tree, a title it has long since lost.

It grows on Bull Creek Flat in Rockefeller Forest, part of Humboldt Redwoods State Park, which holds the largest remaining continuous old-growth coast redwood forest in the world. Its neighbour in the grove, the Giant Tree, is the taller by about four feet on its own sign, though the two were measured 34 years apart. Neither has a published age.

A reader sent us two photographs. One is the sign, half hidden behind sword ferns. The other looks straight up the trunk, a column of grey, deeply furrowed bark with dark scars low down, rising past the crowns of smaller trees into a pale sky. The reader filed it as a giant sequoia; the sign and every source call it coast redwood. It costs nothing to visit, on the trails of the Big Tree Area off Bull Creek.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the wooden sign at its foot reading Tall Tree, measured February 1957. It stands on Bull Creek Flat in Rockefeller Forest, in the same grove as the Giant Tree.

question_meta: The Giant Tree and the Tall Tree in Humboldt Redwoods State Park: how tall they are and where to find them on Bull Creek.
question_answer: The Giant Tree is a coast redwood 363 feet tall, named national champion of its species in 1991, and the Tall Tree measured 359.3 feet in 1957. Both stand in Rockefeller Forest in the Big Tree Area on Bull Creek, free to visit.
question_context: Rockefeller Forest, in Humboldt Redwoods State Park in northern California, is the largest remaining continuous old-growth coast redwood forest in the world. The park began in 1921, when Save the Redwoods League bought land largely from the Pacific Lumber Company. In the Big Tree Area on Bull Creek, the park's own signs give the measurements of two named trees. The Giant Tree was recognised by the American Forestry Association in November 1991 as the national champion coast redwood, 363 feet tall and 53.2 feet round, with an average crown spread of 62 feet. The Tall Tree was measured in February 1957 at 359.3 feet, with a trunk 42 feet round, and redwood writers say it once held the title of the world's tallest known tree. Neither tree has a published age. A reader photographed both and the Tall Tree's sign, and filed them as giant sequoias; the signs name them coast redwoods.

faq.q: How tall is the Giant Tree?
faq.a: 363 feet, about 110 metres, by the park's sign, from its 1991 measurement as national champion coast redwood.
No. Both are coast redwoods, Sequoia sempervirens, as the park's signs say.

faq.q: Does it cost anything to see them?
faq.a: No. Both are on short trails from the Big Tree Area parking on Bull Creek.
